### Overview This dataset shows the locations of dams and the areas covered by the reservoirs that they create upstream. The information used to create this dataset is compiled from a variety of sources, creating a global, harmonized account of dams and reservoirs. The current version maps 7,320 dams that were built as recently as 2017, with a combined storage capacity of 6,864 km³. These include reservoirs with a storage capacity of more than 0.1 km³; smaller dams and reservoirs were added if data was available. The production of this dataset was led by a consortium of partners through the Global Water System Project (GWSP) in Bonn, Germany, and is a joint project of the Earth System Science Partnership (ESSP). ### Methodology Datasets were contributed by 11 participating institutions to serve as the foundation for creating the first version of this dataset. The current version of the dataset adds new dams and reservoirs that were mostly derived from data sources available online. These included national repositories, the Clean Development Mechanism project registry of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), some privately maintained databases like Roller Compacted Concrete Dams, and, for validation purposes, information listed by the International Commission on Large Dams (ICOLD). To consolidate the datasets and improve accuracy, the locations of all dams included in the source datasets were verified, updated, and/or newly georeferenced. This process was guided by maps, atlases, and online resources (including Google Earth). Each dam (with a few exceptions, see source [methodology](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/100125)) was assigned to a polygon that depicts the reservoir surface. In the first version of the dataset, most polygons used for this procedure were provided by the SRTM Water Body Database (SWBD), a near-global, public mapping product created at 30 m resolution from remote sensing imagery. Additional reservoir outlines were added from various alternative sources or digitized from scratch. In the newest version of the dataset, most of the new reservoir polygons that were added were delineated from the surface water maps produced by the Joint Research Center (JRC) of the European Commission from Landsat imagery at 30 m resolution for the period 1984-2015. Cross-validation of the information provided by different sources was performed, and records with suspicious information were flagged and individually verified. Data gaps were filled by comparing and merging attributes from different databases. If inconsistencies, uncertainties, or data gaps remained, the “Quality” index of the record was lowered accordingly. The spatial raster dataset delineates the boundaries of the human settlements at 10m resolution, and describes their inner characteristics in terms of the morphology of the built environment and the functional use. The Morphological Settlement Zone (MSZ) delineates the spatial domain of all the human settlements at the neighboring scale of approx. 100m, based on the spatial generalization of the built-up surface fraction (BUFRAC) function. The objective is to fill the open spaces that are surrounded by large patches of built space. MSZ, open spaces, and built spaces basic class abstractions are derived by mathematical morphology spatial filtering (opening, closing, regional maxima) from the BUFRAC function. ### Overview This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) shows global anthropogenic emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) in 2018 from the following sectors: agriculture, animal agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions. Nitrogen oxides are a family of highly reactive air pollutants, produced by fossil fuel combustion from power plants and gasoline-burning vehicles. Nitrogen oxides are also an important precursor to ground-level ozone (O₃), an air pollutant and a major component of smog, which can worsen bronchitis and asthma and damage lung tissue. “Nitrogen oxides” is used to collectively describe the larger group of similar pollutants, which includes nitrogen dioxide, nitrous acid, and nitric acid. Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). Each compound shows the emissions by sector for up to 11 sectors, depending on the atmospheric compound. The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions dataset was developed by Emissions of Atmospheric Compounds and Compilation of Ancillary Data (ECCAD-AERIS). The data has global coverage at a 0.1 degree resolution, which is approximately 11 kilometers x 11 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Emissions are provided as an annual sum for the years 2000 to 2019. This dataset shows annual emissions for the year 2018. ### Methodology The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions are based on the data provided by the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research version 4.3.2 (EDGARv4.3.2) historical data. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. These trends were then disaggregated onto the same 0.1 degree grid as in EDGARv4.3.2. The sectors were then merged and aligned between the CEDS and EDGARv4.3.2 datasets. The 2011 to 2014 trends were applied to the EDGARv4.3.2 2010 emissions to estimate the emissions up to the year 2018. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/sites/default/files/2019-05/cams_emissions_general_document_apr2019_v6.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). This dataset was developed in 2019 by a team of researchers at the University of Michigan. The map shows the geographic distribution of an index developed to represent the exposure of Mahé’s coastline to the impacts of a storm surge event. Due to the minimal record of storm surge data in Seychelles, the difficulty of gauging how global climate change could increase the probability of a storm surge occurring, and the fact that data parameters typically used in storm surge prediction models weren’t made available to the research team, this data set identifies the regions that would be most exposed to the impacts of a storm surge, rather than the likelihood of a storm surge occurring. Considering these existing constraints, this model is processes-based and not calibrated by existing storm surge data; therefore, it is purely theoretical. The data was created in ArcGIS using a multi-criteria analysis model with elevation, slope, topographic wetness index, cost distance from river, soil type, and vegetation cover as criteria of interest. These variables were scaled, weighted, arranged into a pairwise comparison matrix, assigned relative importance, put into an Analytic Hierarchy Process program to calculate weighted sums, and ultimately produce a storm surge exposure index. A more comprehensive explanation of how this index was created can be found in the report linked below.

### Overview This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) shows global anthropogenic emissions of black carbon in 2018 from the following sectors: agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions. Black carbon is a particulate emitted from the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, biofuels, and biomass. Major [sources include](https://www.c2es.org/document/what-is-black-carbon/) diesel engines, coal-fired power plants, cook stoves, wood burning, and forest fires. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research), black carbon is a “global environmental problem that has negative implications for both human health and our climate.” Inhalation of black carbon is associated with [cardiovascular disease, respiratory problems, cancer, and even birth defects](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research). Black carbon makes up a significant portion of particulate matter pollution. Although black carbon is not a greenhouse gas, it contributes to climate change in a few ways. Its dark color absorbs solar radiation, which warms up the atmosphere. Black carbon also settles on snow and ice, darkening these surfaces that would normally reflect a lot of solar radiation. According to research published in [Nature Geoscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/ngeo473), black carbon may have caused more than 30% of the recent rapid warming in the Arctic. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. The Environmental Impact by Food Type (Calories) data set, produced by World Resources Institute in its 2018 World Resources Report: _Creating a Sustainable Food Future_, illustrates the variations in impact of various food products on land use, freshwater use, and greenhouse gas emissions per million kilocalories consumed. Land use is separated into cropland use and pasture land use. Freshwater use is specified as either from rainwater or irrigation. Greenhouse gas emissions are categorized as occurring during land-use change (e.g., converting forested land to pasture or cropland) or during agricultural production. The impact is measured by the hectares used, thousand cubic meters of freshwater used, or tons of carbon dioxide equivalent produced per million of kilocalories consumed. Both plant-based and animal-based food products are examined in this data set. The plant-based products examined are sugar, rice, rapeseed and mustard seed oil, palm oil, maize, roots and tubers, wheat, soybean oil, fruits and vegetables, sunflower seed oil, and pulses; the animal-based products are pork, eggs, fish (farmed, includes all aquatic animal products), poultry, dairy, beef, and sheep and goat meat. The data set clearly illustrates that animal products overwhelmingly use more land and water, and produce greater quantities of greenhouse gas emissions, than plant-based products. The data used in this data set are global means for land use, water use, and GHG emissions and were derived from the GlobAgri-WRR model (land use and greenhouse gas emissions), authors’ calculations from Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011, 2012) (freshwater consumption), and Waite et al. (2014) (farmed fish freshwater consumption). Freshwater use for farmed fish products is shown as rainwater and irrigation combined. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates are based on a marginal analysis (i.e., additional agricultural land use and emissions per additional million calories or ton of protein consumed). Based on the approach taken by the European Union for estimating emissions from land-use change for biofuels, land-use change impacts are amortized over a period of 20 years and then shown as annual impacts. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates for beef production are based on dedicated beef production, not beef that is a coproduct of dairy. Tons of harvested products were converted to quantities of calories and protein using the global average edible calorie and protein contents of food types as reported in the Food and Agriculture Organization's FAOSTAT (2017). ### Overview The Air Quality: Aerosol Index Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of an index that measures the presence of aerosols that absorb ultraviolet (UV) radiation in the atmosphere, such as dust and smoke. This index may be referred to as the absorbing aerosol index (AAI) or the UV Aerosol Index (UVAI). Absorbing Aerosols are solid and liquid particles suspended in the atmosphere. They are made up of primary aerosols and secondary aerosols. Primary aerosols are emitted directly, whereas secondary aerosols are formed by gases reacting in the atmosphere. Absorbing aerosols are mostly made of dust and smoke. The main sources of aerosols are combustion, like burning biomass, and natural sources, like volcanoes. The AAI can show dust and smoke particles coming from events like dust storms, volcanic eruptions, fires, and biomass burning around the world. The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system.The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as absorbing aerosols, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution. Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO). ### Methodology The TROPOMI AAI dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. UV-absorbing aerosol data was collected by determining the amount of Rayleigh scattering that occured in the UV spectral range for a pair of wavelengths. A spectral range is the range of light wavelengths that a specific spectrometer can measure, and in this case it refers to the wavelength of light that UV-absorbing aerosol molecules emit in the atmosphere. Rayleigh scattering is the scattering of light particles without causing a change in their wavelength. The UV-absorbing aerosol data collected was then compared with a calculated theoretical Rayleigh scattering value based on no UV-absorbing aerosols being present in the troposphere. The difference in scattering between the two data points represents the amount of UV-absorbing aerosols present and is the absorbing aerosol index. A positive AAI value indicates that UV-absorbing aerosols are present. The dataset was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “UV-Aerosol Index”. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO). description: The Global Climate Risk Index identifies the extent to which countries have been affected by extreme weather events. These can be meteorological events such as tropical storms or tornados, hydrological events such as storm surges or flash floods, or climatological events such as wildfires or droughts. The index scores are derived from country’s rankings within the following indicators, and averaged according to their weighting: - Number of deaths – Weight: 1/6 - Number of deaths per 100,000 inhabitants – Weight: 1/3 - Sum of losses in US$ in purchasing power parity (PPP) – Weight: 1/6 - Losses per unit of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) – Weight: 1/3 Lower index scores indicate countries with higher risk. Countries with high ranks in each category (low numbers) add up to low index values. The Global Climate Risk Index has been calculated for impact in 2018 and separately for the annual average impact from the past 2 decades (1999-2018). We recommend using [this dataset](702f4bcb-c376-49b6-9345-cdc8aa989582) as a replacement.**_ The Environmental Impact by Food Type (Calories) data set, produced by World Resources Institute in its 2018 World Resources Report: _Creating a Sustainable Food Future_, illustrates the variations in impact of various food products on land use, freshwater use, and greenhouse gas emissions per million kilocalories consumed. Land use is separated into cropland use and pasture land use. Freshwater use is specified as either from rainwater or irrigation. Greenhouse gas emissions are categorized as occurring during land-use change (e.g., converting forested land to pasture or cropland) or during agricultural production. The impact is measured by the hectares used, thousand cubic meters of freshwater used, or tons of carbon dioxide equivalent produced per million of kilocalories consumed. Both plant-based and animal-based food products are examined in this data set. The plant-based products examined are sugar, rice, rapeseed and mustard seed oil, palm oil, maize, roots and tubers, wheat, soybean oil, fruits and vegetables, sunflower seed oil, and pulses; the animal-based products are pork, eggs, fish (farmed, includes all aquatic animal products), poultry, dairy, beef, and sheep and goat meat. The data set clearly illustrates that animal products overwhelmingly use more land and water, and produce greater quantities of greenhouse gas emissions, than plant-based products. The data used in this data set are global means for land use, water use, and GHG emissions and were derived from the GlobAgri-WRR model (land use and greenhouse gas emissions), authors’ calculations from Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011, 2012) (freshwater consumption), and Waite et al. (2014) (farmed fish freshwater consumption). Freshwater use for farmed fish products is shown as rainwater and irrigation combined. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates are based on a marginal analysis (i.e., additional agricultural land use and emissions per additional million calories or ton of protein consumed). Based on the approach taken by the European Union for estimating emissions from land-use change for biofuels, land-use change impacts are amortized over a period of 20 years and then shown as annual impacts. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates for beef production are based on dedicated beef production, not beef that is a coproduct of dairy. Tons of harvested products were converted to quantities of calories and protein using the global average edible calorie and protein contents of food types as reported in the Food and Agriculture Organization's FAOSTAT (2017). ### Overview This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) shows global anthropogenic methane (CH₄) emissions in 2018 from the following sectors: agriculture, animal agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions. Methane is a powerful, short-lived greenhouse gas, [emitted as a result of](https://scied.ucar.edu/methane) raising cattle and other ruminant animals, rice production, landfills, and energy generation. Methane is also an important precursor to ground-level ozone (O₃), an air pollutant and a major component of smog, which can worsen bronchitis and asthma and damage lung tissue. Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). Each compound shows the emissions by sector for up to 11 sectors, depending on the atmospheric compound. The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions dataset was developed by Emissions of Atmospheric Compounds and Compilation of Ancillary Data (ECCAD-AERIS). The data has global coverage at a 0.1 degree resolution, which is approximately 11 kilometers x 11 kilometers at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Emissions are provided as an annual sum for the years 2000 to 2019. This dataset shows annual emissions for the year 2018. ### Methodology The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions are based on the data provided by the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research version 4.3.2 (EDGARv4.3.2) historical data. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. These trends were then disaggregated onto the same 0.1 degree grid as in EDGARv4.3.2. The sectors were then merged and aligned between the CEDS and EDGARv4.3.2 datasets. The 2011 to 2014 trends were applied to the EDGARv4.3.2 2010 emissions to estimate the emissions up to the year 2018. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/sites/default/files/2019-05/cams_emissions_general_document_apr2019_v6.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). ### Overview The child malnutrition datasat shows child malnutrition estimates for 152 countries in 2018. This dataset demonstrates child malnutrition using five indicators: stunting, wasting, severe wasting, underweight, and overweight among children under 5 years old. The indicators are based on height, weight, and age ratios of children compared to World Health Organization (WHO) Growth Standards. The dataset utilizes the information collected from 854 household nutritional surveys and is presented in tabular format on a global scale. The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), UN World Health Organization (WHO), and World Bank interagency team regularly update this dataset. Malnutrition robs children’s futures and hinders their growth, chance of survival, and development. Ultimately, this severely reduces their ability to contribute to their local communities and the world as a whole. According to UNICEF, nearly half of all deaths in children under five are attributable to undernutrition. Analysis from this dataset reveals that malnutrition rates remain alarmingly high. To improve children’s nutrition requires multi-sectoral programming with long term planning strategies. Regular data collection is essential to monitor trends and progress, and to raise awareness of nutritional problems. ### Methodology This dataset was created using estimates from 854 nationally representative household nutritional surveys that were reviewed against a set of quality control criteria. These surveys are typically carried out every three to five years, so yearly estimates were created using data trends. Survey data was checked for validity and consistency. Additionally, to ensure that survey estimates were comparable over time, survey data was compared to an international standard reference population, the WHO Child Growth Standards. The WHO Child Growth Standards were used to compare five malnutrition indicators to those collected in surveys. Survey data for each indicator was presented using z-scores (how many standard deviations away from the mean) based on the WHO Child Growth Standards. For example, stunting is calculated as the proportion of children with height-for-age below two standard deviation of the reference population based on WHO Child Growth Standards. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://data.unicef.org/resources/dataset/malnutrition-data/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for global and regional level malnutrition, as well as indicator-specific national and disaggregated data are also available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) global anthropogenic shows sulfur dioxide (SO₂) emissions in 2018 for the agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes sectors. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions. Sulfur dioxide is a colorless air pollutant with a strong odor. The gas is a respiratory irritant that can harm human health. According to the [Australian Department of Environment and Energy](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-sulfur-dioxide-so2), sulfur dioxide irritates the nose, throat, and airways. It can cause shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, or a tight feeling around the chest. High concentrations of sulfur dioxide can affect lung function, worsen asthma attacks, and worsen existing heart disease in sensitive groups. Most sulfur dioxide emissions come from the burning of coal, oil, or gas for electricity and transportation; these fossil fuels contain sulfur, which is emitted as sulfur dioxide when burned. Sulfur dioxide does not contribute to global warming, but it reacts easily with other substances to form harmful compounds such as sulfuric acid and small sulfate particles. When sulfur dioxide reacts with water and oxygen, it [creates acid rain](https://www.epa.gov/acidrain/what-acid-rain). Acid rain has a number of [environmental impacts](https://www.ucsusa.org/clean-energy/coal-and-other-fossil-fuels/hidden-cost-of-fossils), including making lakes, rivers, wetlands, and other water bodies more acidic, which can be harmful to fish and other aquatic wildlife. Each compound shows the emissions by sector for up to 11 sectors, depending on the atmospheric compound. CAMS global anthropogenic emissions was developed by Emissions of Atmospheric Compounds and Compilation of Ancillary Data (ECCAD-AERIS). The data has global coverage at a 0.1 degree resolution, which is approximately 11 kilometers x 11 kilometers at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Emissions are provided as an annual sum for the years 2000 to 2019. This dataset shows annual emissions for the year 2018. ### Methodology The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions are based on the data provided by the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research version 4.3.2 (EDGARv4.3.2) historical data. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 x 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. These trends were then disaggregated onto the same 0.1 x 0.1 degree grid as in EDGARv4.3.2. The sectors were then merged and aligned between the CEDS and EDGARv4.3.2 data sets. The 2011 to 2014 trends were applied to the EDGARv4.3.2 2010 emissions to estimate the emissions for the year 2018. For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/sites/default/files/2019-05/cams_emissions_general_document_apr2019_v6.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows CAMS Global Anthropogenic Emissions for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), and [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d). ### Overview The Air Quality: NO₂ Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) density in the troposphere. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of NO₂ between Earth’s surface and the top of the troposphere. The NO₂ density is reported with units of moles of NO₂ per square meter of air (mol/m²). Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is one of the most common compounds in the nitrogen oxides (NOx) group. Other nitrogen oxides include nitric acid (HNO₃) and nitric oxide (NO). NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides, meaning if NO₂ is present it is likely other nitrogen oxides are as well. NO₂ is primarily created by the burning of fuel, which can be from cars, trucks and buses, power plants, and off-road equipment. Breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the human respiratory system. Acute exposures can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms, like coughing, wheezing or difficulty breathing. Longer chronic exposures to elevated concentrations of NO₂ may contribute to the development of asthma and potentially increase susceptibility to respiratory infections. People with asthma, as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂. The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system. The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as NO₂, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution. Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). ### Methodology The TROPOMI NO₂ dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. The data was retrieved and analyzed using a 3 step process. 1. Total NO₂ slant column density was determined from radiance and irradiance spectra measured by TROPOMI. It was analyzed using a Differential Optical Absorption Spectroscopy (DOAS) method. NO₂ slant column density is the amount of NO₂ found along an average path taken by photons traveling from the sun to the satellite sensor. 2. Slant column density data was then separated into stratospheric and tropospheric categories based on information coming from the satellite’s data assimilation system. Stratospheric data was then removed from the dataset. 3. Tropospheric slant column density was converted into tropospheric vertical column density and the average NO₂ density for the entire vertical column was calculated. This was determined by applying an appropriate air mass factor (AMF) and actual, daily information on the vertical distribution of NO₂ calculated by the TM5-MP global chemistry transport model. The altitude-dependent AMF used depended on the satellite geometry, terrain height, cloud fraction and height, and surface albedo. The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Total Column”. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_035_tropomi_atmospheric_chemistry_model). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The GLIMS: Global Glacier Database managed by the NSIDC is an international collaborative project that includes more than 60 institutions worldwide. Its goal is to create this globally comprehensive inventory of land ice including measurements of glacier area, geometry, surface velocity, and snow line elevation. To perform these analyses, the GLIMS project uses satellite data, primarily from the Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) and the Landsat Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+), as well as historical information derived from maps and aerial photographs. The analysis results are submitted to the GLIMS database at the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) in Boulder, CO. The GLIMS database is designed to be a logical extension of the World Glacier Inventory (WGI) of the World Glacier Monitoring Service (WGMS) and stores the full complement of the WGMS-defined glacier characteristics. Each analysis received by the GLIMS team at the NSIDC is ingested into the GLIMS Glacier Database. New glacier data are continually being added to the database. ### Overview The Air Quality: O₃ Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of ozone (O₃) densities in the total atmospheric column. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of O₃ found between Earth’s surface and the top of the atmosphere. The O₃ density is reported with units of moles of O₃ per square meter of air (mol/m²). Unlike stratospheric ozone, which forms naturally in the upper atmosphere and protects us from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays, ground-level (or tropospheric) ozone is created through the interactions of man-made (and natural) emissions of volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides in the presence of heat and sunlight. Cars and gasoline-burning engines are large sources of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). VOCs also come from consumer products such as paints, insecticides, and cleaners as well as industrial solvents and chemical manufacturing. High concentrations of ozone near ground level can be harmful to people, animals, crops, and other materials. Ozone can irritate the respiratory system, causing coughing and irritation. Ozone can aggravate pre existing respiratory problems like asthma, emphysema, and bronchitis and reduce the immune system's ability to fight off infections. Additionally, it can inflame and damage cells that line the lungs. It is possible for ozone to cause irreparable lung damage. These effects can be worse in children and exercising adults. The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system.The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as O₃, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution. Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [carbon monoxide (CO)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). ### Methodology The TROPOMI O₃ dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. O₃ data was collected by determining the amount of radiation reflected by the troposphere in the UV Huggins bands (325-335 nanometers) spectral range of the solar spectrum. A spectral range is the range of light wavelengths that a specific spectrometer can measure and in this case it refers to the wavelength of light that O₃ molecules produce in the atmosphere. The O₃ data collected using this method was then input into the GODFIT (GOME Direct-FITting) algorithm, created by the European Space Agency. Along with O₃ data, the following information was input into GODFIT: - Relative profile of O₃ and sulfur dioxide (SO₂) in the atmosphere for a given region - Estimated surface albedo for the region - Solar/viewing geometry and geo-location of the S5P satellite - Surface pressure, elevation map, snow and ice maps for the earth’s surface, ozone temperature, cloud cover/pressure profiles, and the absorbing aerosol index for the tropospheric column being measured SO₂ profiles were required as SO₂ converts to sulfuric acid in the atmosphere and blocks incoming solar radiation. This interferes with O₃ readings by TROPOMI. The results from GODFIT were analyzed with the convective-cloud-differential method (CCD) combined with cloud measurement data to produce the final dataset. The final result produced was vertical total column density of O₃ (mol/m²). For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Ozone (O₃) Total Column”. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [carbon monoxide] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). description: ### Overview The Transboundary Freshwater Dispute Database (TFDD) catalogs the number and delineation of the world's international river basins and also contains physical, socioeconomic, and political data relating to each of them. In the context of these datasets, an international river basin is defined by its ultimate outlet to an ocean, sea, or inland water body and has year-round flow crossing or drawing a political border. This database includes data at the scale of basins as well as basin country units, which is an area of an international river basin that falls within a particular country. The Relative Risk Category for Hydropolitical Tension estimates the relative level of risk a basin or basin country unit has for political tension over its transboundary rivers. This risk is based on: 1. **water infrastructure development**: the ability to deal with disputes arising from the development of new water infrastructure 2. **institutional vulnerability**: the capacity of a basin country unit to absorb tension, which is expressed by the presence or absence of treaties, treaty provisions, and river basin organizations This data was calculated by TFDD-affiliated researchers as a part of the Governance thematic group within the Transboundary Water Assessment Programme's River Basin Component. ### Methodology The delineation and count of international river basins and basin country units were determined using the [Register of International River Basins](https://transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/content/register-international-river-basins) and watershed boundaries from the [HydroBASINs](https://www.hydrosheds.org/page/hydrobasins) dataset. HydroBASINS provides global coverage of watershed boundaries with several levels of sub-basin delineations, including watersheds that range in scale from tens to millions of square kilometers (see [Lehner & Gill, 2013](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.9740)). For full documentation on the spatial boundary data, please see the [methodology](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/07900627.2019.1572497). Institutional Vulnerability is measured by five components of formal transboundary cooperation. The five components are: 1. at least one water treaty 2. at least one treaty with an allocation mechanism 3. at least one treaty with a flow variability management mechanism 4. at least one treaty with a conflict resolution mechanism 5. at least one river basin organization The presence of a component is summed to give the institutional vulnerability score from 0 to 5, with 0 being the most vulnerable and 5 being the least vulnerable. Relative Risk Category for Hydropolitical Tension is calculated based on the basin country unit's institutional vulnerability score and the presence of a large dam or water diversion project in the basin country unit or upstream of it. If a basin country unit has a lower score for its institutional vulnerability and has infrastructure development in the basin country unit or upstream, it is in a higher risk category for Hydropolitical tension. Relative Risk ranges from 1 (very low risk) to 5 (very high risk). For full documentation on the metrics shown in this dataset, please see the [Transboundary River Basins report](https://transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/sites/transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/files/Database/ResearchProjects/TWAP/GEF_TWAPRB_FullTechnicalReport_compressed.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](6af67024-b917-4944-851a-152b566ff1a8) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview The Maritime Boundaries dataset shows boundaries for exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial seas (TS) and contiguous zones (CZ) for coastal countries around the world. The [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)](http://www.vliz.be/en/imis?module=ref&refid=325469) defined the EEZ, CZ and TS maritime boundaries and coastal baselines. An EEZ is a sea zone over which a country has special rights to explore and use marine resources. Typically, a country’s EEZ extends 200 nautical miles (NM) from its coast (or baseline), unless that distance would overlap with another country’s EEZ. TS are coastal waters that are the sovereign territory of a given country. This zone extends a maximum of 12 NM from a country’s baseline. A CZ is a sea zone that extends an additional 12 NM beyond the outer edge of the TS (up to 24 NM from a country’s baseline). Countries have limited legal rights within the CZ. Data for the Maritime Boundaries dataset was published by the Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ) in 2018 and is available for download from [Marine Regions](https://marineregions.org/). The Maritime Boundaries dataset is a useful tool for managing and displaying marine data. It provides a standardized map of global maritime boundaries. The Maritime Boundaries dataset is useful for linking marine information, such as species distribution lists or coral reef health, to particular countries. The dataset also shows the various jurisdictional reaches of countries. This is important for understanding marine resource management and the rights that countries have to protect their waters. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was generated by the [Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ)](https://www.vliz.be/en), a non-profit organization dedicated to scientific research on the ocean, seas, coasts and tidal estuaries. Based in Belgium VLIZ was established in 1999 by the Flemish government and [the Research Foundation - Flanders](https://www.fwo.be/en/). The central focus of VLIZ is to provide knowledge to the research community, educators, the general public, policymakers and marine industries. ### Methodology The boundaries shown in the Maritime Boundaries dataset were generated from a combination of **normal**, **straight** and **archipelagic** baselines. The UNCLOS defines a **normal** baseline as the low-water line along a country’s coast. A **straight** baseline is a straight line representing the baseline where there is a fringe of islands along the coast, or the coast is heavily indented. **Archipelagic** baselines apply to archipelago countries, which are made of a group of islands. These baselines are straight lines that connect the coastlines and contain the main islands of the country. Normal baselines were drawn using a combination of the [Esri Countries 2014 dataset](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=ac80670eb213440ea5899bbf92a04998) and the [United Nations Environmental Program (UNEP) Coral Reef Distribution dataset](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/1), referred to as the World Countries 2014 dataset. Coral reef data was used to draw baselines for countries where reefs were a fundamental part of their maritime boundaries. Straight and archipelagic baselines were drawn based on [definitions from the UN](https://www.un.org/Depts/los/LEGISLATIONANDTREATIES/regionslist.htm) or maritime treaties and agreements. Countries typically define borders at sea in agreements with their neighbors. These borders were used when available. Median lines were drawn between countries where borders at sea were not specified. Median lines connect points at equal distance from neighboring coastal countries. The baselines were used to generate boundaries of EEZ, TS and CZ sea zones. The boundaries are seaward distances of 200 EEZ, 12 TS and 24 CZ NM from a country’s baseline. Polygons representing the EEZ, TS and CZ areas were calculated using a buffer distance measured from the combination of straight, archipelagic and normal baselines. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was created by merging the EEZ, TS and CZ boundaries with the World Countries 2014 dataset using the [Pairwise Dissolve tool](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/tool-reference/analysis/pairwise-dissolve.htm) in ESRI ArcGIS Pro 2.5.0. Landlocked countries were removed before merging and added in afterward. Differences between coastlines in the EEZ and World Countries 2014 datasets caused small gaps in the polygons. These gaps were fixed in QGis 3.0 using the [Delete Holes tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectorgeometry.html#delete-holes) and the [Difference tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectoroverlay.html#difference). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.marineregions.org/eezmethodology.php). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. VLIZ also provides boundaries of internal waters, archipelagic waters and high seas. ### Overview This dataset includes a comprehensive index for clean energy sector investment in 104 developing nations. These nations include 100 countries that are classified as less developed according to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), along with Chile, Mexico, Turkey, and Qatar, which are important developing nations with emerging clean energy markets. This index, formally known as the Climatescope index, is crucial in showing clean energy investment potential amid rapidly changing market circumstances. This [Climatescope](http://global-climatescope.org/) index is developed by BloombergNEF and supported by the UK Department for International Development. This tool is intended for use by investors, companies, governments, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), researchers, communities, and others seeking to evaluate the opportunities of investing in clean energy. ### Methodology The scores were calculated based on three topics with their associated weights in parentheses: fundamentals (50%), opportunities (25%), and experience (25%). A total of 167 different indicators and subindicators were used to score these topics. Each of the three topics is described below: - **Fundamentals** assessed the fundamental structures that encourage clean energy to prosper. Indicators for *Fundamentals* described a country’s clean energy policies, power sector structure, regulations, and local barriers to renewable energy development. Example indicators included domestic climate change laws, nationally determined contribution (NDC) target coverage, and climate change mitigation incentives. - **Opportunities** analyzed future opportunities for clean energy growth in a country. Indicators for *Opportunities* represented a country’s current and future electricity demand, its energy consumption, carbon dioxide emissions from the power sector, and short- and medium-term opportunities for renewable energy procurement. Example indicators included electrification rate, the growth rate of generation, and upcoming renewable auctions. - **Experience** reflected the track record to host clean energy development successfully in a country. Indicators for *Experience* described a country’s historical levels of renewable energy investment, the comprehensiveness of its nonmanufacturing clean energy value chain, and the volume of installed clean energy. The assumption was that markets with greater experience deploying renewable energy usually offer lower risks for investors. Example indicators included the capacity of clean energy that has been installed, foreign investment in renewables, and the number of clean energy service providers. To collect data, BloombergNEF analysts made 23 countries visits to conduct interviews, in addition to desktop research. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://global-climatescope.org/methodology). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The Environmental Impact by Food Type (Protein) data set, produced by World Resources Institute in its 2018 World Resources Report: _Creating a Sustainable Food Future_, illustrates the variations in impact of various food products on land use, freshwater use, and greenhouse gas emissions per ton of protein consumed. Land use is separated into cropland use and pasture land use. Freshwater use is specified as either from rainwater or irrigation. Greenhouse gas emissions are categorized as occurring during land-use change (e.g., converting forested land to pasture or cropland) or during agricultural production. The impact is measured by the hectares used, thousand cubic meters of freshwater used, or tons of carbon dioxide equivalent produced per ton of protein consumed. Both plant-based and animal-based food products are examined in this data set. The plant-based products examined are wheat, rice, maize, pulses, and roots and tubers; the animal-based products are food pork, eggs, fish (farmed, includes all aquatic animal products), poultry, dairy, beef, and sheep and goat meat. The data used in this data set are global means for land use, water use, and GHG emissions and were derived from the GlobAgri-WRR model (land use and greenhouse gas emissions), the authors’ calculations from Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011, 2012) (freshwater consumption), and Waite et al. (2014) (farmed fish freshwater consumption). Freshwater use for farmed fish products is shown as rainwater and irrigation combined. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates are based on a marginal analysis (i.e., additional agricultural land use and emissions per additional million calories or ton of protein consumed). Based on the approach taken by the European Union for estimating emissions from land-use change for biofuels, land-use change impacts are amortized over a period of 20 years and then shown as annual impacts. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates for beef production are based on dedicated beef production, not beef that is a coproduct of dairy. Tons of harvested products were converted to quantities of calories and protein using the global average edible calorie and protein contents of food types as reported in the Food and Agriculture Organization's FAOSTAT (2017). description: The Global Roads Inventory Project (GRIP) dataset was developed to provide a more recent and consistent global roads dataset for use in global environmental and biodiversity assessment models. The GRIP dataset is mainly aimed at providing a roads dataset that is easily usable for scientific global environmental and biodiversity modelling projects. The dataset is not suitable for navigation. GRIP4 is based on many different sources (including OpenStreetMap) and to the best of our ability we have verified their public availability, as a criteria in our research. The UNSDI-Transportation datamodel was applied for harmonization of the individual source datasets. We have only included included highways, primary and secondary roads as part of this dataset. The original GRIP dataset consists of tertiary and local roads as well.

### Overview The Urban Land Use (Areal) – Mexico dataset provides an estimation of land use land cover (LULC) for nine cities in Mexico. The nine cities are Culiacán, Guadalajara, León, Mérida, Mexico City, Monterrey, Reynosa, Tijuana, and Tuxtla Gutiérrez. Land cover indicates the physical cover over the surface of lands, such as water or vegetation, whereas land use shows how people use the land, such as commercial or plantation. A LULC map classifies areas within a set of categories. This dataset includes the following six categories: Open space, Nonresidential, Residential - Atomistic, Residential - Informal subdivision, Residential - Formal subdivision, and Residential - Housing project. (For full definitions of these categories, see [this working paper](https://marroninstitute.nyu.edu/uploads/content/Measuring_the_Quality_of_Urban_Layouts_December_1_2016_Reduced_new.pdf) or the [technical note](https://www.wri.org/publication/mapping-urban-land-use-in-india-and-mexico).) These "areal" categories exclude the major "linear" urban LULC category: Roads. The data is available for the year 2018 and has a resolution of 5 meters (m). The dataset was produced by the World Resources Institute (WRI). It provides an insight into LULC within cities: what lies where and when. This information can play a critical role in urban planning and monitoring. The dataset can be used to measure the impact of different types of urban land use on air quality or identify what types of land use have been affected by natural disasters. Although this particular LULC dataset captures only one moment in time, when available there is also a high value to change detection over time, looking both forward, for planning purposes, and backward, to chart and understand the outcomes of past pressures, development, and policy decisions. ### Methodology The Urban Land Use (Areal) – Mexico dataset was produced in an automated way via supervised machine learning techniques. Automating urban LULC classification reduced the resource and time requirements by orders of magnitude, relative to manual mapping, thus making the process highly scalable. The machine learning model used for classification required two primary ingredients: satellite imagery and ground-truth data. Ground-truth is the observation or measurements about what actually exists at a specific location.This data was collected from the Atlas of Urban Expansion, a multiphase research effort conducted by the New York University (NYU) Urban Expansion Program in partnership with UN-Habitat and the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy. The Sentinel-2 constellation of the European Space Agency was used as the source of satellite imagery. The original resolution of the imagery was 10 m; this was later upsampled to 5 m to utilize as much information as possible from the ground-truth data. The satellite imagery was combined with the ground-truth data to create training samples required for training the model. The models were relatively small, straightforward convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The trained models were finally used to map selected cities in Mexico. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/mapping-urban-land-use-in-india-and-mexico). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [roads](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e1c519d3-16ea-400a-a71c-9033ba5f490b) for the same nine cities in Mexico and LULC (areal) data for [India](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e354f7b8-0fca-422f-bf12-fc6189812bec). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/mapping-urban-land-use-in-india-and-mexico). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [areal LULC](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/dfbf97c3-ee82-4c68-808b-3bcc60e57167) for the same nine cities in Mexico and for [urban India](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e354f7b8-0fca-422f-bf12-fc6189812bec). _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](ccee0012-de06-433d-8092-8516bdfb79de) as a replacement.**_ The Environmental Impact by Food Type (Protein) data set, produced by World Resources Institute in its 2018 World Resources Report: _Creating a Sustainable Food Future_, illustrates the variations in impact of various food products on land use, freshwater use, and greenhouse gas emissions per ton of protein consumed. Land use is separated into cropland use and pasture land use. Freshwater use is specified as either from rainwater or irrigation. Greenhouse gas emissions are categorized as occurring during land-use change (e.g., converting forested land to pasture or cropland) or during agricultural production. The impact is measured by the hectares used, thousand cubic meters of freshwater used, or tons of carbon dioxide equivalent produced per ton of protein consumed. Both plant-based and animal-based food products are examined in this data set. The plant-based products examined are wheat, rice, maize, pulses, and roots and tubers; the animal-based products are food pork, eggs, fish (farmed, includes all aquatic animal products), poultry, dairy, beef, and sheep and goat meat. The data used in this data set are global means for land use, water use, and GHG emissions and were derived from the GlobAgri-WRR model (land use and greenhouse gas emissions), the authors’ calculations from Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011, 2012) (freshwater consumption), and Waite et al. (2014) (farmed fish freshwater consumption). Freshwater use for farmed fish products is shown as rainwater and irrigation combined. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates are based on a marginal analysis (i.e., additional agricultural land use and emissions per additional million calories or ton of protein consumed). Based on the approach taken by the European Union for estimating emissions from land-use change for biofuels, land-use change impacts are amortized over a period of 20 years and then shown as annual impacts. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates for beef production are based on dedicated beef production, not beef that is a coproduct of dairy. Tons of harvested products were converted to quantities of calories and protein using the global average edible calorie and protein contents of food types as reported in the Food and Agriculture Organization's FAOSTAT (2017). Based on global sea level rise scenarios, researchers at the University of Michigan mapped which parts of the Seychellois island of Mahé would be inundated by 0.5, 1, 1.5, and 2 meters of sea level rise. High to low tides vary by about 2 meters in Seychelles; to account for additional inundation from high tides, an additional 1 meter was added to each of the sea level rise scenarios. Using elevation data, the researchers mapped which sections of the coastline are expected to be flooded in the event of the given amount of sea level rise. The data was developed in 2019.

### Overview The Air Quality: CO Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of carbon monoxide (CO) densities in the total atmospheric column. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of CO found between Earth’s surface and the top of the atmosphere. The CO density is reported with units of moles of CO per square meter of air (mol/m²). Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas that can be harmful when inhaled in large amounts. CO is released during combustion, so the largest outdoor sources of CO are cars, trucks and other vehicles, and machinery that burn fossil fuels. Breathing air with a high concentration of CO reduces the amount of oxygen that can be transported in the bloodstream to critical organs like the heart and brain. At very high levels, which are possible indoors or in other enclosed environments, CO can cause dizziness, confusion, unconsciousness, and death. Very high levels of CO are not likely to occur outdoors. However, when CO levels are elevated outdoors it can be of particular concern to people with preexisting heart disease. These people already have a reduced ability for getting oxygenated blood to their heart. They are especially vulnerable to the effects of CO when exercising or under increased stress. In these situations, short-term exposure to elevated CO may result in reduced oxygen to the heart accompanied by chest pain also known as angina. The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system.The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as CO, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution. Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). ### Methodology The TROPOMI CO dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. CO data was collected by determining the amount of sunlight reflected by the troposphere in the 2.3 µm spectral range of the solar spectrum. A spectral range is the range of light wavelengths that a specific spectrometer can measure and in this case it refers to the wavelength of light that CO molecules produce in the atmosphere. The CO data collected using this method was then input into the Shortwave Infrared CO Re- trieval (SICOR) algorithm created by the Netherlands Institute for Space Research. Along with CO data, the following information was input into SICOR: - Relative profile of CO and water in the atmosphere for a given region - Solar/viewing geometry and geo-location of the S5P satellite - Temperature, water vapor/pressure profiles, and geo-potential height of the S5P satellite - Estimate of methane (CH₄) abundance as calculated by the TM5-MP global chemistry transport model CH₄ estimates were required as CH₄ is used to help filter out the presence of clouds in the model. The algorithm further takes into consideration cloud cover by changing the column sensitivity (altering the minimal amount of light reflection within the column required to determine CO density) according to the light path created by cloud cover. The final results produced by the algorithm were tropospheric vertical column density of CO and the average CO density for the entire vertical column. The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Carbon Monoxide (CO) Total Column”. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_035_tropomi_atmospheric_chemistry_model). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: Disclaimer This resource is currently being under revision. A preprint is available at: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-6343364/v1 The data is available at three resolutions: 1000 m: this deposition 100 m: see related datasets below 20 m: Only on Google Earth Engine (also 1000 m and 100 m available): LAI: ee.ImageCollection('/ee-speckerfelix/assets/open-earth/lai_predictions-mlp_20m_v01') FAPAR: ee.ImageCollection('/ee-speckerfelix/assets/open-earth/fapar_predictions-mlp_20m_v01') FCOVER: ee.ImageCollection('/ee-speckerfelix/assets/open-earth/fcover_predictions-mlp_20m_v01') GEE-App: Open GEE App Visualization Code: Open in GEE Code Editor Example: Mosaicking / Scaling / Filtering Code: Open in GEE Code Editor Abstract Environmental restoration projects are crucial for ecosystem recovery and biodiversity conservation but monitoring progress at a global scale poses substantial challenges. Publicly funded satellite missions such as Sentinel-2 have great potential to transform ecosystem monitoring due to their high spatial and temporal resolution if they can be reliably linked to ecosystem characteristics. Here, we present the first global, analysis-ready, decametric maps for three key vegetation biophysical properties on an annual basis, including effective leaf area index (LAIe), fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR), and fractional vegetation cover (FCOVER). We utilize a hybrid retrieval approach of the physically based radiative transfer model PROSAIL to directly estimate biophysical variables from multispectral Sentinel-2 images, making use of multiple observations during the peak of the growing season. All retrievals are aggregated into mean values, standard deviations, and the number of observations taken during this period. The maps are available at 20 m, 100 m, and 1000 m spatial resolution for the years 2019 to 2024, totaling approximately 20 TB of analysis-ready data, and are validated using in-situ data from the Ground-Based Observations for Validation (GBOV). The annual temporal and decametric spatial resolution of these maps provides new opportunities for biodiversity and ecosystem monitoring, enabling more effective assessments of restoration efforts and contributing to the development of standardized global monitoring frameworks. Description This data set includes: Annual Effective Leaf Area Index (LAIe) (2019 - 2024): Includes annual mean (mean of retrievals), variation (standard deviation of retrievals) and count (number of cloud-free observations) for LAI at 1000, and 100 m resolution. Annual Fractional Vegetation Cover (FCOVER) (2019 - 2024): Includes annual mean (mean of retrievals), variation (standard deviation of retrievals) and count (number of cloud-free observations) for FCOVER at 1000, and 100 m resolution. Annual fraction of absorbed photosynthetically activate radiation (FAPAR) (2019 - 2024): Includes annual mean (mean of retrievals), variation (standard deviation of retrievals) and count (number of cloud-free observations) for FCOVER at 1000, and 100 m resolution. Higher-resolution 20-meter maps are only available on Google Earth Engine (see this link). Data Format and Scaling Data Types: Mean and standard deviation maps are stored as int16. Count maps are stored as uint8. NoData Values: Mean and standard deviation maps: -9999 Count maps: 255 Scaling Factors (applies only for int16 maps): FAPAR and FCOVER: 0.0001 LAI: 0.001 Children depositions (100 m versions) To download all at once, you can use the following bash script: Link GitHub LAI Mean 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 Std / Count 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 FAPAR Mean 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 Std / Count 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 FCOVER Mean 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 Std / Count 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 Code The code used to generate the data is available at Zenodo, and at the GitHub repository. Naming Convention To ensure consistency and ease of use across and within the projects, we follow the standard Open-Earth-Monitor file-naming convention. The convention works with 10 fields that describe important properties of the data. In this way, users can search files, prepare data analysis etc, without needing to open files. The fields are: Variable name: [lai, fapar, fcover] Method: rtm.mlp (Radiative transfer model inversion, using multi-layer perceptron regression model) Position in probability distribution: [mean, std, count] Spatial resolution: [20m, 100m, 1000] Depth reference or depth interval s ("s": surface) Time reference begin: 20190101 Time reference end: 20191231 Bounding box: go (global land without Antarctica) Coordinate reference system: epsg.4326 World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS 84) Version Code: v1 Contact Felix Specker: felix.specker@usys.ethz.ch / speckerfelix@gmail.com Johan van den Hoogen: johan.vandenhoogen@usys.ethz.ch

description: These datasets consist of estimated daily surface NO2 concentrations over Europe at ~1km spatial resolution in tiff file format generated using S-MESH model and is part of the research article https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2024.114321. Files are zipped into 3 folders each corresponding to a year and can be unzipped from command line using "tar -xvzf filename.tar.gz". Each file represents surface NO2 during the Sentinel-5P satellite overpass time, and the file is named based on the date of measurement. Each tiff file is a single band image with an extent of 25°W-42.5°E & 29.9-74.28°N in EPSG:4326 - WGS 84 projection. The surface NO2 concentrations are estimated using Sentinel-5P TROPOMI tropospheric column density and a XGBoost machine learning model. The overall median absolute error of the model predictions across Europe is 4.43μg/m3 Summary Data: NO2 concentrations over Europe at ~1km spatial resolution Time Period: 2019-2021 Methodology: Using satellite, reanalysis and other relevant data, and XGBoost machine learning model

The data is available at three resolutions: 1000 m: This deposition (global mosaics as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs) 100 m: See related datasets below 20 m and full 100 m products: Available on Google Earth Engine (GEE): LAIe: ee.ImageCollection('projects/ee-speckerfelix/assets/open-earth/laie_predictions-mlp_20m_v03') FAPAR: ee.ImageCollection('projects/ee-speckerfelix/assets/open-earth/fapar_predictions-mlp_20m_v03') FCOVER: ee.ImageCollection('projects/ee-speckerfelix/assets/open-earth/fcover_predictions-mlp_20m_v03') Earth-Engine App: https://ee-speckerfelix.projects.earthengine.app/view/global-trait-maps Earth-Engine Visualisation Script: Open in GEE Code Editor Earth-Engine Analysis Script: Open in GEE Code Editor Abstract We present S2BIOPHYS, a global dataset of annual vegetation biophysical properties derived from Sentinel-2 imagery at 20 m and 100 m resolution for 2019–2025. The dataset includes effective leaf area index (LAIe), fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR), and fractional vegetation cover (FCOVER), estimated using a radiative transfer model inversion approach calibrated with in-situ data. Annual composites are generated from peak growing-season observations and include per-pixel mean values and uncertainty estimates. Global mosaics (EPSG:4326) are provided at 100 m and 1000 m resolution as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs, with full-resolution products and extended uncertainty information available via Google Earth Engine. The dataset supports applications in ecosystem monitoring, biodiversity assessment, and restoration analysis. Description This dataset provides global annual composites of vegetation biophysical properties derived from Sentinel-2 data. The Zenodo archive contains global mosaics in geographic coordinates (EPSG:4326) at 1000 m resolution (this deposition) and 100 m resolution (child datasets). Annual Effective Leaf Area Index (LAIe) (2019–2025): Ensemble mean and total uncertainty (standard deviation) Annual Fractional Vegetation Cover (FCOVER) (2019–2025): Ensemble mean and total uncertainty (standard deviation) Annual Fraction of Absorbed Photosynthetically Active Radiation (FAPAR) (2019–2025): Ensemble mean and total uncertainty (standard deviation) Each product represents an annual composite based on multiple Sentinel-2 observations during the peak growing season. Resource Description This Zenodo record provides global annual composites of LAIe, FAPAR and FCOVER for 2019–2025 as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs). The data are distributed as global mosaics in geographic coordinates (EPSG:4326) at 1000 m spatial resolution (this deposition), with additional 100 m products available as separate Zenodo records. Each product contains the ensemble mean and total uncertainty derived from multiple Sentinel-2 observations during the peak growing season. These datasets are designed to be analysis-ready and easily accessible for large-scale applications. The full dataset is available on Google Earth Engine (GEE) at 20 m and 100 m resolution in Sentinel-2's native UTM projection: ee.ImageCollection("projects/ee-speckerfelix/assets/open-earth/{laie, fapar, fcover}_predictions-mlp_{100,20}m_v03") The GEE products additionally provide observation counts ([laie, fapar, fcover]_count) and a decomposition of uncertainty into within-acquisition ([laie, fapar, fcover]_stdDev_within) and across-acquisition ([laie, fapar, fcover]_stdDev_across) components, enabling more detailed uncertainty analysis and quality filtering. In addition to these annual products, we provide the gee-biophys Python package, which enables users to generate custom spatiotemporal composites. It implements both S2BIOPHYS and SL2P and allows users to define time intervals, spatial extents, and resolution using a simple configuration file, supporting reproducible and scalable generation of biophysical maps. This framework also enables access to the full set of uncertainty components at native resolution where required.
